items.questionAndWhy: Can people learn that foods they already like predict negative outcomes, or do those preferences interfere with updating new information?
items.whatTheyDid: Rich and colleagues tested 279 participants in two cohorts using a probabilistic learning task. Personally liked and disliked foods were paired with outcomes that either confirmed or contradicted existing preferences, and the order of those blocks was varied.
items.whatTheyFound: Predictions were more accurate when outcomes matched existing preferences (about 68% versus 61%). Starting with confirming evidence made subsequent learning less flexible, especially for liked foods. Positive associations were learned more readily than negative ones. The authors caution that outcomes were artificial points rather than real eating consequences.
items.whatItMeans: Early confirmation of a preference can change how later counterevidence is learned. This is useful for thinking about message or training sequence, but the experiment did not demonstrate dietary behavior change or establish that the same effect applies to political beliefs.
items.streamTitle: Confirming an existing food preference first made later counterevidence harder to learn
items.streamSummary: Two cohorts totaling 279 people learned probabilistic outcomes associated with foods they personally liked or disliked. Accuracy was higher when outcomes matched prior preferences, and starting with a confirming block made later updating less flexible. Positive associations were generally easier to learn than negative ones. The experiment shows how starting conditions and prior preferences interact during associative learning, not that a particular diet intervention will work. The consequences were artificial points and no real food consumption outcome was tested.

items.questionAndWhy: Does feeling anxious make people disengage from mentally demanding tasks, and does a person’s usual anxiety level change that relationship?
items.whatTheyDid: Sayalı, Heling and Cools tested two online samples (107 and 572 participants) using tasks and self-reports of engagement. They measured trait anxiety and examined state anxiety, including an affective-state manipulation in the second experiment.
items.whatTheyFound: Their predicted anxiety-by-difficulty pattern was not supported. In the first experiment, higher state anxiety tracked lower engagement mainly on easy tasks among people low in trait anxiety; in the second, the attenuation among higher-trait-anxiety participants partly replicated but was not limited to easy tasks.
items.whatItMeans: The relationship between acute anxiety and effort is not one uniform effect. Baseline differences and task context matter, while the inconsistent difficulty interaction limits claims about when anxiety produces disengagement.
items.streamTitle: Acute anxiety reduced task engagement less consistently among people with higher trait anxiety
items.streamSummary: Two online experiments involving 107 and 572 participants tested how current anxiety, typical anxiety levels, and task difficulty jointly relate to engagement. Contrary to the authors’ main hypothesis, higher state anxiety predicted less engagement primarily among low-trait-anxiety participants, with the task-difficulty pattern changing between experiments. The study offers evidence against a simple claim that anxiety always increases effort avoidance. Findings partly replicated, but engagement measures and the inconsistent difficulty interaction limit how precisely the effect can be generalized.

items.questionAndWhy: Does parenting influence childhood anxiety, does child anxiety change parental behavior, or do both processes operate together?
items.whatTheyDid: Yap, Cardamone-Breen and Rapee reviewed evidence on reciprocal parent–child associations and examined how child-anxiety interventions address parental behavior and family interactions.
items.whatTheyFound: The review identifies evidence consistent with influences in both directions, involving factors such as parental overprotection and children’s behavioral inhibition. It emphasizes that many interventions and studies do not fully capture these interrelationships. It does not offer one pooled causal estimate or show that every observed association reflects parent-to-child causation.
items.whatItMeans: A family process may contain feedback rather than a simple one-way influence. For causal-model builders, within-family longitudinal evidence and intervention evidence should be kept distinct from cross-sectional associations.
items.streamTitle: A new review treats child anxiety and parenting as a two-way relationship, not a one-way cause
items.streamSummary: A Nature Reviews Psychology article synthesizes research on relationships between parenting and childhood anxiety, including overprotection, behavioral inhibition, and parent-focused interventions. The authors argue that children and parents can influence one another, so a model that always places parenting upstream of child anxiety may be incomplete. They also identify gaps in how intervention studies measure these relationships. This is a research review rather than a new randomized experiment, and reciprocal association does not by itself settle the causal direction or size of any particular pathway.
items.attribution: Yap, Cardamone-Breen & Rapee — Nature Reviews Psychology

items.questionAndWhy: How can analysts map a complex workforce problem while distinguishing a factor’s position in a hierarchy from its overall driving influence?
items.whatTheyDid: Sahran and colleagues used Total Interpretive Structural Modeling (TISM), literature review, stakeholder consultation and MICMAC analysis to organize 21 potential contributors to job–training mismatch among Malaysian technical and vocational graduates.
items.whatTheyFound: Labor-market conditions, socioeconomic background and gender occupied the same lower hierarchical level, but MICMAC classified the first two as driving factors and gender as relatively autonomous. Personal interests were also classified as driving despite their different hierarchical position. These are structured interpretive judgments, not estimated causal effects.
items.whatItMeans: Two network summaries can answer different questions. Hierarchical location should not be interpreted as proof of causal leverage or intervention feasibility; this paper is a useful example of combining participatory structure with explicit analytic distinctions.
items.streamTitle: Hierarchical position and driving influence disagreed in a participatory workforce model
items.streamSummary: Researchers mapped 21 proposed causes of graduate job mismatch in Malaysia using Total Interpretive Structural Modeling and MICMAC analysis. The results showed why model interpretation matters: labor-market conditions and socioeconomic background were classified as drivers, while gender shared their hierarchical level but was not classified the same way. Personal interests also had high driving power despite a different level. The study provides an organized map of expert and literature-derived judgments, not observational identification of causal effects. It is especially useful for avoiding mistaken interpretations of network hierarchy as intervention priority.
items.attribution: Sahran, Ashaari & Ali Othman — Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

items.questionAndWhy: Does a combined AI-assisted instructional architecture improve computational-thinking scores over conventional teaching?
items.whatTheyDid: Zhang and Wang built an integrated system for educational resources, adaptive learning paths, interactive support and multi-dimensional evaluation, and tested it for 14 weeks with 120 university students in two intact classes.
items.whatTheyFound: The AI-assisted class scored higher on a composite computational-thinking measure (Cohen’s d about 0.97). But each treatment condition was assigned to one entire class, so class and treatment effects cannot be separated. Adjusting for student pretest scores does not resolve that design problem.
items.whatItMeans: The architecture is a practical design prototype, not clean evidence of a generalizable treatment effect. Repeated classes, cluster randomization and independently scored transfer tasks would provide stronger next tests.
items.streamTitle: AI-assisted teaching showed a large classroom difference, but treatment was confounded with class
items.streamSummary: A 14-week university pilot compared an AI-assisted teaching package with ordinary teaching across 120 students in two intact classes. The AI class scored substantially higher on the study’s computational-thinking composite (Cohen’s d approximately 0.97), particularly for abstraction and evaluation. However, one class received each condition, making teacher, peer and class-level differences inseparable from the intervention. The authors explicitly frame this as a two-class feasibility pilot. The result is worth testing further, not evidence that the specific AI system caused an effect of that size.

items.questionAndWhy: Who can detect and investigate harm when AI-generated health guidance is delivered privately through chatbots or inserted into search and social feeds?
items.whatTheyDid: DeVerna and colleagues published a perspective mapping two exposure routes—incidental encounters with AI health content and deliberate questions to AI systems—and assessing accountability gaps. They proposed user-accessible records, incident reporting, independent evaluation and platform-level mitigation.
items.whatTheyFound: The authors identify an observability gap: many harmful or misleading interactions are not visible to clinicians, researchers or regulators. This is an analytical argument supported by prior literature, not a new prevalence estimate or experiment demonstrating the effectiveness of the recommended controls.
items.whatItMeans: The central PSYWERX relevance is measurement infrastructure. Without records linking exposure, guidance, later decisions and outcomes, neither behavioral effects nor incident rates can be assessed reliably.
items.streamTitle: AI health misinformation may be hard to measure because the harmful interaction stays inside a platform
items.streamSummary: A Nature Health perspective argues that generative AI has made health information more accessible while leaving major gaps in external visibility. People may encounter generated advice through search, social media or private chatbot conversations, but clinicians and researchers often cannot inspect what was said or what followed. The authors recommend portable conversation records, incident-reporting routes, independent evaluation and stronger accountability. These are governance proposals rather than experimentally validated remedies. The important analytic insight is that effects cannot be assessed well when exposure, guidance and downstream behavior are invisible.

items.questionAndWhy: How is the U.S. Army’s future missile-defense capability being developed against faster and more maneuverable threats?
items.whatTheyDid: Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge on October 9 as its candidate for the Army’s Future Interceptor program. The company describes a new seeker, Northrop Grumman multi-pulse motor, upgraded flight controls and planned integration with existing launch and battle-command systems.
items.whatTheyFound: The Army advanced the company into the next development stage, and Lockheed Martin plans testing in 2027 toward potential deployment by 2031. The announcement gives intended capabilities but no independent flight-test, intercept-probability or cost-effectiveness results for PAC-3 Edge.
items.whatItMeans: The item marks a technology-development and industrial transition, not demonstrated hypersonic-intercept performance. Follow-on evidence should include representative tests, sensor-to-intercept reliability, integration and manufacturing output.
items.streamTitle: PAC-3 Edge enters Army interceptor development, with testing still planned for 2027
items.streamSummary: Lockheed Martin unveiled PAC-3 Edge on October 9 for the U.S. Army’s Future Interceptor competition. It proposes a redesigned seeker, multi-pulse motor and flight-control improvements intended to extend defended range and altitude while connecting to existing air-defense systems. The company says testing is scheduled to begin in 2027 with possible deployment by 2031. This is a program and design milestone, not demonstrated effectiveness: no independent PAC-3 Edge flight-test results, intercept rates, or field cost data were released. Subsequent testing will determine whether the proposed advantages materialize.

items.questionAndWhy: How can export controls on advanced AI servers be bypassed in practice, and what has moved from allegation to an admitted criminal act?
items.whatTheyDid: According to an October 9 Reuters report based on a federal court filing, broker Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun pleaded guilty on October 8 to four counts connected with diverting restricted AI servers to China. Earlier DOJ allegations describe third-country routing, false end-user paperwork and staged dummy servers.
items.whatTheyFound: The guilty plea establishes Sun’s admission to offenses including export-control and smuggling conspiracies; it does not establish guilt for other defendants. Prosecutors described approximately $2.5 billion in server orders tied to the wider alleged scheme. Super Micro says it was not a defendant.
items.whatItMeans: This is a concrete supply-chain deception and enforcement case. Analysts should distinguish charged conduct, admitted conduct, alleged scheme scale and organizational responsibility rather than treating the entire indictment as proven.
items.streamTitle: AI-server export diversion case advanced from an indictment to a contractor’s guilty plea
items.streamSummary: A contractor linked to AI-server manufacturer Super Micro pleaded guilty in Manhattan federal court on October 8 to four charges tied to attempts to divert restricted U.S. AI servers to China. An earlier Justice Department account described fake documentation, third-country routing and dummy servers used to deceive inspections, with roughly $2.5 billion in orders associated with the alleged wider scheme. The plea is important new evidence, but does not determine the guilt of other charged individuals or prove every allegation about the scheme’s scale. Super Micro itself is not a defendant.

items.questionAndWhy: Can a routine chest X-ray help identify people who might need a dedicated bone-density scan, reducing unnecessary testing without missing many osteoporosis cases?
items.whatTheyDid: Kim and colleagues trained a chest-radiograph model on 46,478 paired X-ray and DXA examinations from 26,757 patients. They externally tested it in three independent cohorts of 6,391, 24,132 and 122,535 people and simulated referral thresholds.
items.whatTheyFound: Osteoporosis-detection AUROC was about 0.88 in one external hospital cohort and 0.92–0.93 in two screening cohorts. A retrospective simulation suggested DXA use could fall by around half while retaining 98–99% of osteoporosis cases, but the clinical workflow was not prospectively tested.
items.whatItMeans: This is promising triage evidence with unusually broad external validation. Prospective referral outcomes, subgroup performance, prevalence differences and the consequences of missed low-bone-density cases remain important.
items.streamTitle: A chest-X-ray AI model screened for osteoporosis across three external cohorts
items.streamSummary: Researchers trained an AI model using more than 46,000 paired chest X-rays and bone-density scans, then validated it in three separate cohorts. Osteoporosis-detection AUROC ranged from about 0.88 to 0.93. A simulation suggested that AI-guided prescreening could reduce dedicated DXA scanning by roughly 50% while still identifying 98–99% of osteoporosis cases. The projected reduction in scans is not a measured clinical outcome: referral decisions and patient consequences were not tested prospectively. It is a strong illustration of the difference between discrimination, simulated workflow benefits and field effectiveness.
items.attribution: Kim et al. — npj Digital Medicine

items.questionAndWhy: Can a real-time AI scribe produce better clinical records while preserving factual accuracy?
items.whatTheyDid: Du and colleagues developed SMART-ASSISTANT, combining consultation audio transcription, structured notes, quality checking and diagnostic assistance. They evaluated abdominal-pain documentation in simulated, retrospective, clinician-reader and prospective comparisons.
items.whatTheyFound: In the prospective cohort, AI records were rated more complete or intact (3.50 versus 3.21) but less factual (3.34 versus 4.01) than physician records. Other quality dimensions showed no significant differences. The study did not show that better documentation ratings improved patient outcomes.
items.whatItMeans: A tool can gain on completeness and lose on correctness at the same time. Evaluation must score these separately and preserve clinician review, especially before inaccurate details enter the durable medical record.
items.streamTitle: AI-generated clinic notes were more complete but less factual than physician notes
items.streamSummary: SMART-ASSISTANT combines audio transcription, structured medical-record drafting, quality checks and diagnosis support. In a prospective outpatient comparison, its notes scored higher on completeness or integrity than physician-written notes (3.50 versus 3.21), but significantly lower on factuality (3.34 versus 4.01). Other assessed dimensions showed no clear difference. The mixed result is more useful than a single headline quality score: fluent, complete documentation may still contain incorrect statements. The study supports supervised evaluation of clinical scribes, not autonomous acceptance of their records or evidence of improved patient outcomes.

items.questionAndWhy: How much AI deployment in radiation oncology has reached sustained, monitored clinical operation in lower-resource settings?
items.whatTheyDid: Ndassi and colleagues systematically reviewed six databases for work published through December 2025, finding 18 eligible studies from low- and middle-income settings. They rated each study on a staged spectrum from readiness to sustained integrated operation.
items.whatTheyFound: Two studies addressed readiness only, nine reported task-level applications, six described clinician-supervised integration, and one reported coordination across workflow stages. None supplied enough evidence for the highest sustained-operation category; continuous monitoring was not reported.
items.whatItMeans: Proof of an algorithmic task is not the same as a functioning health service. Readiness needs evidence on infrastructure, workforce fit, workflow integration, continuous monitoring and governance, not simply model accuracy.
items.streamTitle: Only one of 18 low-resource radiation-oncology studies showed multi-stage AI integration
items.streamSummary: A systematic review of 18 studies from low- and middle-income settings assessed how far radiation-oncology AI has progressed from isolated model tasks to sustained clinical operation. Nine studies were task-level demonstrations, six showed clinician-supervised workflow integration, and only one described coordination across workflow stages. None met the review’s highest operational category, and continuous performance monitoring was not reported. This is a deployment-maturity assessment rather than proof that the systems are ineffective. It highlights infrastructure, validation, personnel and governance as barriers between successful prototypes and reliable clinical services.
items.attribution: Ndassi et al. — npj Digital Medicine
